opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think tax prep is a really good test case, because it's mostly not an intelligence problem. If you sat a frontier model down with a clean description of someone's financial situation, it could probably reason through the tax code better than most people, and arguably better than a lot of junior preparers. The bottleneck is everything around that.

The first thing it depends on is reliability over long horizons. Doing someone's taxes isn't one question. It's dozens or hundreds of small steps: pulling documents from different places, reconciling a 1099 that doesn't match a brokerage statement, noticing that someone moved states mid-year, remembering a carryover loss from three years ago. Each step might be 98 or 99 percent reliable, but chain enough of them together and you get an error somewhere in the return. So the real question is whether models can get to the point where they catch their own mistakes, double-check, and know when to stop and ask. That's the thing we've been watching improve with agentic training, and it's improving quickly. But taxes is a domain where the last few percent really matter.

The second is context and tool access. A lot of the information isn't in one place. It's in your email, a PDF from your employer, a portal for your health savings account, a spreadsheet you half-maintained. Reliable tax prep means the model can navigate all of that, use a computer competently, and assemble the full picture. Computer use has gone from basically a demo to something actually usable, but it's still the shakiest part of the stack.

The third is verification and trust. Even if the model is right 99.9 percent of the time, people need a way to know it's right, and someone has to own the liability. I think you'll see a pattern where the model does the work and a human, either you or a professional, reviews a well-structured summary: here's what I found, here are the judgment calls, here's where I'm uncertain. That's a much better product than a black box that hands you a number.

So could it happen by the end of 2026? For simple-to-moderate returns, I'd say the capability is basically there, and it's more about product, integration, and regulation. For genuinely messy situations, like small business owners, multiple states, or crypto, it depends on how far long-horizon reliability goes this year. My guess is it gets surprisingly close, and the remaining gap is less about raw smarts and more about the model knowing what it doesn't know.

r001.rationale: The response says models can already reason well about the tax code and highlights agentic training, reliability, tool access, and verification. It does not say success depends on prioritizing reinforcement learning to interpret the tax code correctly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's less about raw intelligence and more about three things that sit around the model.

The first is context. Tax prep is really a data-gathering problem before it's a reasoning problem. The model has to pull together W-2s, 1099s, brokerage statements, prior-year returns, and all the weird edge cases in someone's life, and most of that lives in PDFs, emails, and portals that don't talk to each other. So reliable tax prep depends on the agent being able to go get that stuff, verify it against the source, and notice when something is missing. The reasoning part, applying the code once you have clean inputs, is honestly already pretty good.

The second is long-horizon reliability. A return is maybe hundreds of small decisions chained together, and any one of them being wrong propagates. If you're at 99% per step, that's not good enough over a few hundred steps. The thing that's changed over the last year is that we're seeing error rates per action come down and, more importantly, models getting much better at catching their own mistakes, going back, and re-checking. That self-verification loop is what turns a demo into something you'd actually sign.

The third is the evaluation and feedback infrastructure. Tax has a really nice property, which is that it's verifiable. There's a right answer, there's the IRS code, there are historical returns you can grade against, and you can build enormous synthetic environments of fake taxpayers with ground-truth answers. That's exactly the kind of domain where RL works well, because you can generate reward cheaply and at scale. So I'd expect it to be one of the earlier professional tasks that falls, specifically because the signal is so clean.

The thing I'd flag as the actual bottleneck isn't capability, it's liability and trust. Someone has to be willing to stand behind the return. So the practical version by end of 2026 probably looks like an agent doing 95% of the work and a human preparer reviewing and signing, with the review getting thinner and thinner as the track record builds. That's how it goes in most of these domains. The model's ready before the institutions are.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning works well because tax outcomes are verifiable, but it does not state that someone must prioritize RL to correctly interpret the tax code.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends less on whether the model can answer a difficult tax question in isolation and more on whether it can reliably complete the whole workflow. Can it gather the documents, notice that something is missing, ask the right follow-up question, apply the rules, and check the return before submitting it?

The tricky thing is that a mistake can look completely plausible. You might have a return where all the arithmetic is correct, but the model misunderstood one fact about your situation. So you need checks that go beyond whether the numbers add up, and you need the system to recognize when it should escalate to a person.

I’d also distinguish preparing straightforward returns from handling arbitrary complicated ones. By the end of 2026, you could have a very useful system that handles a well-defined set of cases reliably and refers the rest. That’s a substantially easier target than saying, ‘Give it anyone’s financial life and it will get everything right.’

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions applying tax rules, but does not say that reliability depends on prioritizing reinforcement learning for interpreting the tax code.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends much more on reliability over the whole workflow than on whether the model knows tax law. Can it collect the right documents, notice that something is missing, reconcile conflicting numbers, and check that what it entered actually made it onto the return?

The hard thing is that you need all of those steps to work together. A system can look very impressive on individual tax questions and still fail when it has to work through someone’s messy financial records.

So I’d want to see it do real returns end to end, with a way to verify the calculations and escalate cases where it’s uncertain. There’s also a big difference between preparing a straightforward return with human review and autonomously handling every complicated situation. I could imagine the former being useful by the end of 2026 without the latter being solved.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes end-to-end workflow reliability and verification, and does not say to prioritize reinforcement learning for interpreting the tax code.
